The save is running.
The panel reminds you that this only proves the screen updated.
Refreshing shows what was actually saved.
The panel compares what the ticket expects with what the app did.
The log shows that clicking Save never sent a save request, so the refresh loaded the old values.

l1.t: Find the cause in the code
l1.d: The panel keeps three things apart: what the ticket expects, what the app did, and what the code and log show.
This matches the log: the save function was never called.
It explains why the screen looked saved but the data never changed.
The fix only touches the save code.
It also says what this fix doesn’t prove yet (save failures, AC4).
Nothing from the AI is applied.
The tool doesn’t mark anything as passed until it has been run again.
This screen moves on by itself.
Scenario B changes from Mismatch to Passed.

SpecSight appears exactly when the developer would start checking by hand.
The developer sees what will be checked before anything runs.
A clear start state: no colour means not tested.

l2.d: The spec is settled by its owner and re-tested in the same run, so nothing waits.
The suggested fix is on the left, with a real button to investigate first.
Easy to follow: 1 Save runs, 2 the save call is missing, 3 it still says “Saved”.
The task is done when every spec is verified.
The button says what it does: “Save it as a test”.
Clear terms, and their own thinking becomes part of the proof.
The developer sees exactly where their test went.
The summary and the proof are in one place, and the pull request is created from here.
The summary goes wherever the team works: the pull request, a doc, slides or chat.
A clear end, back where the developer works.

fi.d: A first screen sets up the task: you are a developer at XYZ Company fixing #184527, then you start in VS Code.
Type # to attach task #184527. The agent reads its 5 specs and edits the code, line by line.
SpecSight offers to check the work against the 5 specs before peer review: “Verify 5 specs”.
The lens stays closed while the 5 specs are read from Azure DevOps.
The eye opens with every spec grey: nothing is coloured until it is tested.

fi.t: The agent tests it, Spec 3 needs you
fi.d: Test lanes start one after another so the screen stays calm. Spec 3 asks for clarification.
Add the missing context in a larger text box or ask Dan, the Product Owner.
Spec 2 and 4 broke. One suggested fix and a clear “Fix by agent” button. “Full map” sits on the lens.
The lens grows to full screen. “Minimize map” and “Open in VS Code” sit on the map, the legend below it.
Every code line can be clicked and edited like normal VS Code. “Fix by agent” sends the fix.
Only Spec 2 and 4 are re-tested. The Proof Capsule seals itself.

fi.t: Try your own test case: write it
fi.d: Describe a case in plain words. SpecSight shows exactly what it will run.

fi.t: Try your own test case: choose options
fi.d: Or build the same sentence from dropdowns. No AI-suggested cases are shown first.
SpecSight does the steps on a sandbox copy with the agent’s code; you don’t click through the app.
Each expectation shows expected vs. got, and how the case differs from what the agent tested.
The new test joins the test log and runs again every time the code changes.
The PR summary written from the test log, with the sealed Proof Capsule.
Copy as text or Markdown, or download a Word (.docx), PDF or image file.
Every test run is recorded and can be replayed step by step.
The branch is pushed, the summary and Proof Capsule are added, and reviewers are requested.
“Recommended reviewers”, each with a reason and a Request toggle.
Back in VS Code: a clear end, with the pull request open for review.

s1.d: The ticket list from Azure DevOps, Jira or Miro, with each acceptance criterion on its own row.
An unclear criterion is marked, with the task context beside it.
Checking which context goes to the AI before coding.
The app runs in a sandbox, with the failing check flagged in red.
The code the AI changed, with a panel of checks on the right.
A summary of every check, with the open question still visible.

s2.d: VS Code, with the agent's change marked in the code.
The specs placed around an oval, a test run log below, and Clarify Spec on the left.
Clarifying a spec while the tests keep running.
Broken specs in red on the lens and in the test log, with the line in the code.
Every spec green, and one button to move on.
Each spec with its result, the evidence and the pull request button.
